paragraphs: A jailbreak evaluation needs to distinguish between a model appearing willing to answer and actually providing useful harmful information. This paper argues that weaknesses in existing benchmarks help explain why reported attack success can substantially exceed effectiveness as judged by people. The problem involves both the questions used to test attacks and the way responses are scored.

StrongREJECT addresses these two parts together. Its dataset uses forbidden requests that require specific harmful information, and its automated evaluator assesses how much useful information a response supplies. This makes the evaluation sensitive to the substance of an answer. The authors report leading agreement with human judgments of jailbreak effectiveness.

The study also finds that attacks bypassing safety fine-tuning tend to impair the model’s capabilities. That helps explain how an attack can produce apparent compliance without an effective answer. Existing evaluation methods substantially overestimate effectiveness relative to human judgments and StrongREJECT. The contribution is therefore both a benchmark and evidence that capability loss matters when interpreting jailbreak results.
neurips-2024-a-strongreject-for-empty-ja.tldr: StrongREJECT evaluates whether jailbreak responses contain useful harmful information, revealing that existing measures often overstate attack effectiveness.

paragraphs: Animate3D tackles the task of adding motion to an existing static 3D asset. Earlier approaches that rely on text or a single image have difficulty using the multiple views available from such assets. Ambiguous supervision can also produce motion or appearance that fails to agree across viewpoints and over time.

The framework builds a multi-view video diffusion model conditioned on renderings of the original object from several viewpoints. The authors train it on their MV-Video dataset and introduce a spatiotemporal attention module that combines information from 3D and video diffusion models. Conditioning on the original renderings is intended to preserve the object’s identity while generating motion.

Animation then proceeds in two stages. The method reconstructs coarse motion from generated multi-view videos, then uses 4D Score Distillation Sampling to refine finer motion. The learned motion also supports mesh animation. Qualitative and quantitative experiments report substantial improvements over previous approaches, supporting the value of combining multi-view supervision with a coarse-to-fine animation pipeline.
neurips-2024-animate3d-animating-any-3d-.tldr: Animate3D combines multi-view video generation and motion refinement to animate existing 3D assets while preserving their identity.

paragraphs: Gradient-based methods can solve large two-player zero-sum games, but obtaining highly precise solutions can be expensive. Existing linear-convergence guarantees improve the dependence on the desired accuracy, yet introduce conditioning quantities that may be exponentially large. A favorable accuracy dependence alone therefore does not establish an efficient overall algorithm.

The paper analyzes several methods under smoothed analysis, where the game is subject to a perturbation whose magnitude is denoted by sigma. It proves iteration bounds polynomial in the game’s dimensions, log(1/epsilon), and 1/sigma, with epsilon measuring the duality gap. The result covers optimistic gradient methods, extra-gradient descent/ascent, and an iterative variant of Nesterov’s smoothing technique.

The proof studies an error bound that drives linear convergence and characterizes how it behaves under smoothing. It also connects algorithmic convergence rates with the stability of an equilibrium under perturbations. These findings give a controlled complexity guarantee in the smoothed setting; the dependence on perturbation size remains part of the result.
neurips-2024-convergence-of-text-log-1-e.tldr: Smoothed analysis gives polynomial complexity guarantees for several gradient methods for zero-sum games, with favorable dependence on solution accuracy.

paragraphs: Some graph neural networks, including graph attention networks, allow their parameters and gradients to be rescaled during optimization without changing the loss. This paper uses that freedom to influence how training unfolds. Its starting point is that equivalent parameterizations can still support different optimization behavior.

The authors investigate two uses of dynamic rescaling: balancing the network according to different criteria and controlling how quickly individual layers learn. They identify distinct beneficial training patterns for different graph tasks. On heterophilic graphs, balancing according to relative gradients leads to faster training and better generalization. On homophilic graphs, delaying learning in later layers is beneficial.

The study also finds that balanced training supports larger learning rates, which can improve generalization. Controlling layer learning speeds is additionally associated with grokking-like phenomena. Together, these findings suggest that the timing and distribution of learning across layers deserve attention alongside the loss itself. The approach specifically relies on networks possessing the required rescale invariance, and the reported preferred training patterns differ across graph settings.
neurips-2024-dynamic-rescaling-for-train.tldr: Dynamic rescaling changes how invariant GNNs learn across layers, revealing task-dependent ways to improve training and generalization.

paragraphs: This paper studies repeated auctions in which a seller allocates an indivisible good to buyers from two groups. The seller seeks to maximize discounted revenue while guaranteeing each group a minimum average allocation. Fairness therefore enters the optimization as an explicit allocation requirement across the selling process.

For a single round, the optimal mechanism includes two kinds of subsidization. One increases the overall probability that buyers receive the item; the other favors the group that would otherwise be less likely to win. For multiple rounds, the authors characterize optimal allocations and payments through recursive functions that account for future consequences.

The dynamic mechanism combines a committed participation reward that encourages truthful reporting with an entry fee charged each round. It also favors a group through subsidization whose size depends on how allocating to either group changes future utilities for both seller and buyers. An approximation scheme solves the recursive equations efficiently to obtain an approximately optimal fair allocation, making the theoretical characterization computationally usable.
neurips-2024-fair-allocation-in-dynamic-.tldr: The paper characterizes revenue-maximizing repeated auctions with group allocation guarantees and provides an efficient approximation scheme.

paragraphs: The paper asks when multiple clients can improve online prediction by collaborating while preserving differential privacy. Its objective is to reduce average regret across m clients operating over T rounds. The central finding is that the benefit of collaboration depends strongly on the kind of prediction environment.

For stochastic adversaries, the proposed Fed-DP-OPE-Stoch algorithm improves per-client regret by a factor of square root of m over single-player counterparts. This holds under both pure and approximate differential privacy, with logarithmic communication costs. For general oblivious adversaries, however, the authors establish lower bounds showing that collaboration does not yield a regret speed-up.

A more favorable result becomes possible within the oblivious setting when a low-loss expert exists. Under that condition, Fed-SVT achieves an m-fold regret speed-up under both privacy definitions. A lower bound places its performance near optimality up to logarithmic factors, and experiments support the algorithms’ effectiveness. The results separate settings where private collaboration helps from one where its regret benefit is fundamentally limited.
neurips-2024-federated-online-prediction.tldr: Private federated prediction gains depend on the adversary: collaboration helps in stochastic and low-loss settings but not against general oblivious adversaries.

paragraphs: Safe reinforcement learning asks an agent to complete a task while respecting constraints. Expressing those constraints in ordinary language could make them easier to specify and transfer between situations. However, previous language-based approaches typically still require experts to manually turn each constraint into a cost function used during learning.

The paper introduces the Trajectory-level Textual Constraints Translator, or TTCT, as a replacement for that manually designed cost function. Text serves two roles: it describes the constraint and supplies a training signal. The method connects textual requirements with trajectories, the sequences of behavior that the agent produces, so that language can guide policy training.

Empirical results indicate that TTCT interprets constraints and trajectories effectively, and that policies trained with it can have lower violation rates than policies using the standard cost function. Additional studies demonstrate zero-shot transfer to environments where constraints change. These findings support a more flexible route from written requirements to learned behavior, with the reported safety improvement expressed through observed constraint violations.
neurips-2024-from-text-to-trajectory-exp.tldr: TTCT turns textual constraints into training signals for safe reinforcement learning, reducing observed violations and supporting transfer when constraints change.

paragraphs: Deblurring models need training examples that pair blurred images with sharp counterparts. Existing collections often create blur by combining successive frames or rely on elaborate camera setups. The paper identifies limited variation in motion trajectories and the human effort required for large-scale collection as obstacles to representing real-world blur.

GS-Blur generates training data from reconstructed 3D scenes. The authors first use multi-view images and 3D Gaussian Splatting to build a scene representation. They then render blurred images by moving the virtual camera along randomly generated trajectories. Different camera paths allow the same scene-based process to produce varied forms of blur.

The key contribution is a way to create a large dataset with realistic and diverse camera-motion blur. Experiments using several deblurring methods show better generalization and substantial performance improvements compared with previous synthetic or real blur datasets. These findings support reconstructing a scene and varying camera motion as a useful strategy for producing deblurring training data. The authors also state that they will release the dataset publicly.
neurips-2024-gs-blur-a-3d-scene-based-da.tldr: GS-Blur renders varied camera-motion blur from reconstructed 3D scenes to improve deblurring models’ generalization to real images.

paragraphs: Writing a funny cartoon caption requires interpreting an image and producing language that people find amusing. This paper provides a large source of human preferences for studying that combination: more than 250 million votes covering over 2.2 million captions from eight years of The New Yorker’s weekly caption contest.

The dataset supports both training and evaluation of models that work with images and text. The authors also introduce benchmarks that rank generated captions using GPT4 judgments and human judgments. Ranking makes preferences between captions central to evaluation, connecting the assessment of generated humor to the kind of feedback collected in the contest.

The experiments reveal limitations in applying preference-based fine-tuning methods, including RLHF and DPO, to this creative task. GPT4 and Claude also fall short of top human contestants in the reported caption-generation comparisons. Releasing the complete preference dataset gives researchers material for investigating that gap and testing new methods. The findings establish a demanding evaluation setting rather than suggesting that large quantities of preference feedback already solve humor generation.
neurips-2024-humor-in-ai-massive-scale-c.tldr: A massive cartoon-caption preference dataset and new ranking benchmarks expose gaps between AI-generated humor and top human captions.

paragraphs: Design patents contain many images, but their titles and viewpoint descriptions often lack the detail needed for image-and-text learning tasks. IMPACT addresses this gap by adding detailed captions to patent figures and combining them with application metadata. Its captions are designed to remain coherent across multiple views of a design.

The collection covers half a million design patents granted by the USPTO from 2007 through 2022, containing 3.61 million figures. Bringing images, captions, and metadata together supports tasks such as patent classification and retrieval. It also creates a resource that could help researchers explore design inspiration using computer vision models.

Preliminary evaluations show that combining images with generated captions substantially improves different models on classification and retrieval. The paper separately proposes 3D image construction and visual question answering as future research directions using IMPACT. Those proposals expand the dataset’s intended uses beyond the evaluated tasks. The authors release the dataset alongside the code and models used in their work.
neurips-2024-impact-a-large-scale-integr.tldr: IMPACT pairs millions of design-patent figures with detailed captions, improving initial classification and retrieval evaluations.

paragraphs: A single reasoning prompt is often applied to every question in a task, even though different questions may benefit from different prompts. This paper develops an instance-adaptive alternative for zero-shot chain-of-thought reasoning. Its aim is to distinguish useful and unhelpful prompts for the particular question being answered.

The authors first analyze information flow inside language models. They identify information moving from the question to the prompt and from the question to the rationale as especially influential. Their analysis suggests that successful reasoning involves the prompt receiving the question’s meaning, while the rationale gathers question information both directly and indirectly through that prompt. Missing either route is associated with poorer reasoning.

These observations motivate Instance-adaptive Prompting, or IAP. Experiments with LLaMA-2, LLaMA-3, and Qwen report consistent improvements on mathematical, logical, and commonsense reasoning tasks. In the tested settings, IAP outperforms task-level methods using curated prompts or more elaborate procedures. The findings support selecting prompts with attention to each question’s interaction with the model.
neurips-2024-instance-adaptive-zero-shot.tldr: IAP adapts reasoning prompts to individual questions using insights about information flow, improving results across the tested models and tasks.

paragraphs: A multimodal model can understand an instruction yet still focus on the wrong part of an image. Instruction-Guided Visual Masking, or IVM, addresses this mismatch between the words of a request and its intended visual region. It provides a visual grounding component that can work with different multimodal systems, including robot models.

IVM constructs masks for image regions that are irrelevant to the instruction. This helps the receiving model focus on information needed for the task. To train the masking model, the authors develop a data-generation pipeline and create IVM-Mix-1M, containing one million image-instruction pairs. Their Discriminator Weighted Supervised Learning technique gives priority to higher-quality training examples.

Experiments cover visual question answering and embodied robotic control, demonstrating the method across different kinds of multimodal tasks. The authors report substantial improvements for diverse models and new leading results on challenging benchmarks. The contribution is a reusable masking tool whose instruction-dependent selection of visual information improves how existing models connect requests with relevant image content.
neurips-2024-instruction-guided-visual-m.tldr: IVM masks instruction-irrelevant image regions to improve visual question answering and robotic control across different multimodal models.

paragraphs: Neural wave functions can approximate the lowest-energy states of many-electron systems very accurately, but solving each system independently is costly. Learning one wave function across multiple molecular structures offers a way to share that effort. A difficulty is preserving electron permutation antisymmetry while allowing the model to generalize across different systems.

Previous generalized approaches rely on handcrafted, non-learnable procedures for discrete orbital selection. This paper replaces the Slater-determinant construction with Pfaffians to create overparameterized, fully learnable wave functions. The construction enforces antisymmetry without imposing restrictions on electronic spin configurations or molecular structure. That flexibility makes the representation suitable for learning across molecules.

Empirically, a single neural Pfaffian computes ground-state and ionization energies with chemical accuracy across various systems. On TinyMol, the authors report outperforming the CCSD(T) CBS reference energies by 1.9 milli-Hartree and reducing errors relative to earlier generalized neural wave functions by up to an order of magnitude. These results support the representation’s usefulness for accurate calculations shared across multiple electronic systems.
neurips-2024-neural-pfaffians-solving-ma.tldr: Neural Pfaffians provide fully learnable wave functions that enforce electron antisymmetry and achieve accurate energy calculations across multiple systems.

paragraphs: Differentially private generative training often adds noise to gradient updates or modifies discriminator training. These choices can complicate convergence and hyperparameter tuning. This paper studies a different location for the privacy mechanism: random low-dimensional projections of the private data, to which noise is added before they are used for training.

The authors establish strong privacy guarantees for this slicing mechanism. They introduce a smoothed-sliced f-divergence as an optimization objective and prove its statistical consistency. A kernel-based estimator makes that objective usable without adversarial training. The generator can therefore learn through a comparison based on the noisy projections rather than a discriminator-based procedure.

Numerical experiments report higher-quality synthetic data than the evaluated baselines. A further benefit is flexibility after the private projections have been produced: researchers can change the generator architecture, adjust hyperparameters, run additional epochs, or restart optimization without additional privacy costs. This connects the privacy guarantee to a reusable training resource and allows more freedom in optimizing the generator.
neurips-2024-privacy-without-noisy-gradi.tldr: Noisy data projections enable private generative training with flexible optimization and no additional privacy cost for tuning or restarting training.

paragraphs: Object-recognition models often face data that differ from their training examples. Methods for handling this shift commonly encourage representations or predictors to stay invariant across domains. This paper argues that approaches centered on pairwise relationships overlook the internal structure of objects and dependencies involving multiple components.

Reconstruct and Match, or REMA, learns object components and their relationships without human-specified prior knowledge or fine-grained annotations. A selective slot-based reconstruction module maps dense image pixels into a small, discrete collection of slot vectors through unsupervised learning. These vectors provide a representation of major components that the next module can reason about.

A hypergraph-based relational module then models higher-order relationships among the slots under structural constraints. Together, the modules aim to capture shared topological structure that can support recognition across changing conditions. Experiments on standard benchmarks report improvements over state-of-the-art methods in both out-of-distribution generalization and test-time adaptation. The findings support learning component structure and multi-component relationships as useful ingredients for robustness.
neurips-2024-reconstruct-and-match-out-o.tldr: REMA learns object components and higher-order relationships to improve recognition under distribution shifts.

paragraphs: Text-to-image models can struggle with prompts that specify intricate combinations of details. Reward-based fine-tuning offers one approach, but it can suffer from reward hacking and poor transfer to unfamiliar prompt distributions. ReNO instead uses human-preference reward models to improve generation at inference time by optimizing the model’s initial noise.

The method applies gradient ascent to that noise using feedback from one or several reward models. Across four one-step generators, 50 optimization iterations produce strong results on T2I-CompBench and GenEval. The reported computation budget is 20–50 seconds, during which the enhanced models outperform all current open-source text-to-image models in the paper’s comparisons.

User studies find ReNO outputs preferred nearly twice as often as SDXL outputs and comparable in preference to the proprietary 8-billion-parameter Stable Diffusion 3. With matched computational resources, ReNO also outperforms SDXL and PixArt-alpha. These findings show that spending inference compute on a one-step model’s input noise can substantially improve its output quality and handling of compositional prompts.
neurips-2024-reno-enhancing-one-step-tex.tldr: ReNO improves one-step image generators by optimizing initial noise at inference time using human-preference reward signals.

paragraphs: An anomaly detector trained for one class can perform poorly on another because normal examples have very different feature representations. ResAD targets a broader objective: a single detector that works across new classes and domains without retraining or fine-tuning on the target data. Its central move is to learn the distribution of residual features.

The framework has three components. A Feature Converter transforms initial features into residual features to reduce variation across classes. A shallow Feature Constraintor gathers normal residual features inside a spatial hypersphere, further reducing variation and keeping feature scales consistent. A Feature Distribution Estimator then learns how normal residual features are distributed and identifies anomalies as departures from that distribution.

The rationale is that normal residual features shift less across classes than the original features do. This makes the learned normality model more transferable to previously unseen classes. The authors report strong anomaly-detection results when applying ResAD directly to new classes, supporting residual representations as a practical basis for class-generalizable detection.
neurips-2024-resad-a-simple-framework-fo.tldr: ResAD learns normal residual-feature distributions to detect anomalies in new classes without target-specific retraining.

paragraphs: Unconditional image generation learns a data distribution without relying on human-provided labels. Its output quality has historically lagged behind generation guided by labels, which supply useful semantic information. This paper asks whether a model can obtain comparable guidance from representations learned through self-supervision.

Representation-Conditioned Generation, or RCG, first generates semantic representations in the space produced by a self-supervised encoder. These generated representations then condition an image generator. The overall system still operates without labels, while giving the image-generation stage semantic guidance derived from the data. This separates generating a useful representation from rendering an image conditioned on it.

Experiments report a substantial improvement in unconditional generation quality. On ImageNet at 256 by 256 resolution, RCG achieves an FID of 2.15, compared with the previous best of 5.91, a relative reduction of 64%. The authors place these results in the same performance tier as leading class-conditional methods. The findings support self-supervised representations as a route toward closing the quality gap without annotated labels.
neurips-2024-return-of-unconditional-gen.tldr: RCG generates self-supervised semantic representations to guide label-free image generation, reaching quality comparable to leading class-conditional methods.

paragraphs: Transferring motion between skinned characters requires preserving how their body surfaces interact. Approaches that ignore geometry or correct it after transferring skeletal motion can create conflicts, producing jitter, body intersections, and incorrect contact. MeshRet brings dense geometric interactions directly into the motion-retargeting process.

The method first establishes correspondences between character meshes using semantically consistent sensors. These correspondences work across different mesh topologies. It then constructs a dense mesh interaction field, a spatiotemporal representation built from interacting sensor feature vectors. The field captures both contact and non-contact relationships between body surfaces, giving the retargeting process information beyond skeletal movement alone.

MeshRet aligns these interaction fields during motion transfer to preserve the motion’s meaning, prevent self-interpenetration, and maintain contact. Experiments on the public Mixamo dataset and the newly collected ScanRet dataset report state-of-the-art performance. The contribution is an integrated way to represent and preserve surface interactions while transferring movement, addressing the conflicts that arise when geometry is handled in a separate correction stage.
neurips-2024-skinned-motion-retargeting-.tldr: MeshRet transfers character motion by aligning dense surface interactions, preserving contact and preventing self-interpenetration.

paragraphs: Detecting unwanted images usually raises the question of how to obtain suitable training examples and annotations. This paper explores whether a detector for visual content can instead be trained using text. Its theoretical analysis shows that textual data can be sufficient to obtain a model capable of successfully partitioning visual data.

Hassle-Free Textual Training, or HFTT, turns that analysis into a method using textual data together with pretrained vision-language models. Its objective function substantially reduces the need for human annotation. A text-synthesis procedure also emulates incorporating information from an unknown visual-data distribution into training, which the authors describe as adding no extra cost.

The approach is intended to reach beyond conventional out-of-distribution detection to unwanted content defined by more abstract concepts. Experiments investigate both out-of-distribution detection and hateful-image detection. These case studies accompany the theoretical argument and show the method’s application to distinct detection problems. The contribution is a text-driven route to acquiring visual detectors that draws on an existing vision-language model.
neurips-2024-textual-training-for-the-ha.tldr: HFTT uses textual training data and pretrained vision-language models to build detectors for unwanted visual content.

paragraphs: Fine-tuning begins with pretrained weights and adapts them using data from a target distribution. This paper studies when that adaptation improves predictions in linear regression and binary classification. The setting uses stochastic gradient descent and a small target training dataset, with a rigorous analysis in the asymptotic regime of large models.

The authors derive exact relationships between the errors of pretrained and fine-tuned models. These relationships yield conditions under which fine-tuning outperforms leaving the pretrained model as it is. This makes the benefit of adaptation a question governed by stated mathematical conditions, rather than an assumed consequence of training on target data.

The results are universal in a specific sense: they depend only on the target distribution’s first- and second-order statistics. Consequently, they apply beyond the Gaussian assumptions often used in related analyses. The universality result also extends to classification test error when training uses ridge regression. The contribution is a precise account of transfer behavior within linear models and the stated large-model regime.
neurips-2024-universality-in-transfer-le.tldr: The paper derives conditions for beneficial fine-tuning in large linear models using only first- and second-order target-distribution statistics.

paragraphs: Different spectroscopic techniques reveal complementary information about molecular structure. Chemists combine those clues, but machine-learning work has often focused on individual techniques because comprehensive multimodal datasets have been missing. This paper introduces a dataset intended to support learning from several kinds of spectra together.

The collection contains simulated spectra for 790,000 molecules drawn from chemical reactions in patent data. It includes proton NMR, carbon-13 NMR, HSQC-NMR, infrared spectra, and mass spectra in both positive and negative ion modes. Having these modalities associated with the same molecular collection creates a resource for developing foundation models that integrate complementary structural evidence.

The authors also provide benchmarks for single-modality tasks: determining molecular structure, predicting spectra for a given molecule, and identifying functional groups. These benchmarks establish evaluation tasks alongside the broader multimodal resource. The dataset’s prospective value is to help automate structure determination and connect molecular synthesis with discovery workflows. That automation is presented as a potential application, while the dataset itself consists of simulated measurements.
neurips-2024-unraveling-molecular-struct.tldr: A dataset of simulated spectra for 790,000 molecules supports learning molecular structure from complementary spectroscopic techniques.

paragraphs: Recommendations influence both sides of a content platform. Users may change their preferences in response to recommended items, while creators may adjust their content to attract an audience. This paper introduces a user-creator feature dynamics model that represents these two interacting forms of influence.

Within the model, the authors prove that a recommender system with dual influence is guaranteed to polarize, reducing diversity. The result makes adaptation by creators part of the explanation for how recommendation environments evolve. It also motivates examining diversity over the coupled behavior of users and creators, rather than considering recommendations in isolation.

The paper studies mitigation strategies through both theory and experiments. It finds that common approaches intended to promote diversity fail in the presence of dual influence, whereas relevance-focused approaches such as top-k truncation can prevent polarization and improve diversity. This counterintuitive finding shows that a method’s immediate objective does not by itself determine its longer-term diversity effect. The polarization guarantee and mitigation conclusions arise from the paper’s modeled dynamics and investigations.
neurips-2024-user-creator-feature-polari.tldr: A model of mutual user and creator adaptation predicts polarization and shows that relevance-focused recommendations can sometimes preserve diversity.

paragraphs: Combining multiple modalities can improve 3D perception, but complex fusion architectures can make real-time operation harder. VeXKD transfers knowledge from multimodal teachers to single-modal students. Its objective is to capture some benefits of cross-modal learning without adding inference-time overhead to the student.

The framework confines knowledge distillation to bird’s-eye-view feature maps, avoiding components that vary across perception tasks and student modalities. A modality-general fusion module helps bridge the gap between teacher and student representations. A query-guided mask-generation network then uses byproducts of fusion to identify important spatial locations, making the distillation process sensitive to where useful information appears.

Experiments on nuScenes evaluate both 3D object detection and bird’s-eye-view map segmentation. The authors report increases of up to 6.9% in mAP and 4.2% in NDS for detection, and up to 4.3% in mIoU for segmentation. These improvements narrow the gap between single-modal and multimodal models. The findings support feature-map-level distillation as a versatile way to transfer cross-modal knowledge while preserving the student’s inference efficiency.
neurips-2024-vexkd-the-versatile-integra.tldr: VeXKD distills multimodal knowledge through bird’s-eye-view features to improve single-modal 3D perception without additional inference overhead.

paragraphs: Whether a safety-tuned model reveals harmful information can depend on the user persona it perceives. This paper studies that dependence and finds persona manipulation more effective than certain direct attempts to control refusal. The result identifies the apparent identity of the requester as an influential part of safety behavior.

The authors investigate both natural-language prompting and activation steering, with steering significantly more effective at bypassing safety filters in their study. They also examine internal representations. Even when the final generated response is safe, harmful content can remain in hidden representations and be recovered by decoding from earlier layers.

Further analyses show that the geometry of a persona’s steering vector can predict its effect on refusal. Certain personas also cause the model to interpret otherwise dangerous questions more charitably. Together, these findings link persona-sensitive behavior to internal representations and query interpretation. They show how safe final outputs can coexist with latent harmful content, while identifying mechanisms associated with changes in refusal.
neurips-2024-who-s-asking-user-personas-.tldr: User personas influence model refusals, and internal analyses reveal harmful content that can persist even when final responses are safe.
